paragraphs: Sequential exploration gathers information to answer a question about an uncertain environment. This paper studies a version in which an algorithm only needs to identify an option whose expected reward is within a specified tolerance, epsilon, of the best. Several answers can therefore be correct, making the choice of which answer to verify part of the problem.

The authors show that always targeting the option with the highest mean prevents an algorithm from attaining asymptotically optimal expected sample complexity. They instead identify a preferred target called a furthest answer. The important distinction is between finding the highest reward and choosing an acceptable answer that supports the most efficient verification strategy.

Using this insight, the paper gives a simple procedure for adapting best-arm identification algorithms to epsilon-best-answer identification in transductive linear stochastic bandits. It also proposes an asymptotically optimal algorithm and reports competitive empirical performance against modified existing methods. Thus, allowing approximate answers changes both the stopping goal and how an efficient algorithm should choose its candidate.
icml-2022-choosing-answers-in-epsilon-be.tldr: Choosing which acceptable answer to verify enables asymptotically optimal identification of approximately best options in linear bandits.

paragraphs: FINN learns physical processes that evolve over space and time by combining neural networks with structure from numerical simulation. It targets advection-diffusion processes and represents the constituent parts of their partial differential equations compositionally. This lets learned components operate within a model organized around the physical process.

The authors evaluate FINN on several one- and two-dimensional equations, including Burgers’, diffusion-sorption, diffusion-reaction, and Allen–Cahn equations. They report better modeling accuracy and strong generalization outside the training distribution, including across initial and boundary conditions. Across the tested cases, FINN outperforms both purely learned models and other physics-aware approaches, sometimes by multiple orders of magnitude, while using one tenth as many parameters on average.

The paper also examines sparse real-world observations of a diffusion-sorption process. FINN outperforms a calibrated physical model and reveals an unknown retardation factor associated with the observed process. This result suggests explanatory potential alongside predictive accuracy: the compositional structure can help recover a meaningful physical quantity while learning from limited observations.
icml-2022-composing-partial-differential.tldr: FINN combines learned equation components with physical simulation structure, achieving strong accuracy and generalization across the reported physical modeling tasks.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embedding methods learn representations while handling potentially huge collections of entities. Negative sampling is an important part of this training, but performance depends on choices such as the loss margin and the number of negative samples. Finding suitable settings through repeated experiments can consume substantial computation.

This paper analyzes the negative sampling loss to explain how these choices interact with different scoring methods. Its central finding distinguishes methods whose scores have restricted value ranges from those whose scores do not. Restricted-range methods, including TransE and RotatE, require margin or negative-sample adjustments that differ from those appropriate for RESCAL, ComplEx, and DistMult. The scoring function therefore matters when selecting training settings.

The authors also propose subsampling methods designed specifically for this loss and grounded in their theoretical analysis. Experiments on FB15k-237, WN18RR, and YAGO3-10 produce results consistent with the theory. The contribution is a more principled basis for tuning and using negative sampling, connecting practical training behavior to mathematical properties of the embedding model.
icml-2022-comprehensive-analysis-of-nega.tldr: The paper explains how knowledge graph scoring functions affect negative sampling settings and develops theoretically motivated subsampling methods.

paragraphs: Some privacy attacks on language models generate text and then try to identify passages memorized from training. This paper investigates how repeated material in web-scraped training data contributes to those attacks. The authors find that duplication accounts for a large part of the success of the attacks they examine.

The relationship between repetition and regeneration is stronger than proportional. A sequence appearing ten times in training is, on average, generated one thousand times as often as a sequence appearing once. The authors also find that existing methods for detecting memorized sequences perform near chance on training sequences that were not duplicated. These observations connect attack effectiveness to both how frequently text reappears and how well attackers can recognize it.

Removing duplicate training material makes the evaluated language models considerably more secure against these types of attacks. The findings support deduplication as a practical priority for privacy-sensitive applications and motivate reconsidering how effective existing attacks are under different data preparation choices. The demonstrated improvement concerns the studied attacks rather than a general guarantee of privacy.
icml-2022-deduplicating-training-data-mi.tldr: Repeated training text strongly increases regeneration and privacy-attack success, while deduplication substantially reduces the studied risks.

paragraphs: Quantiles describe positions within a dataset’s ordered values, allowing a distribution to be summarized through selected cutoffs. This paper considers the task of estimating several requested quantiles while preserving differential privacy. The objective is to keep those estimates close to the true quantiles while meeting the privacy requirement.

The authors introduce Approximate Quantiles, or AQ, a simple recursive algorithm for this task. They provide a worst-case upper bound on its estimation error, giving a theoretical assessment of accuracy alongside the privacy property. This matters because the algorithm is intended to release multiple useful distribution summaries under a shared requirement to protect the underlying data.

The empirical evaluation finds substantially lower error than previous implementations across several datasets. AQ also runs two orders of magnitude faster than the best previous implementation in the reported comparison. The results therefore show an improvement in both accuracy and computation for the evaluated setting. The combination of a worst-case error bound and favorable measured performance provides complementary evidence for the proposed algorithm.
icml-2022-differentially-private-approxi.tldr: AQ recursively estimates private quantiles with a worst-case error bound and reports lower error and much faster execution than previous implementations.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation and learning use recorded decisions and outcomes to assess or improve policies without fresh online experiments. Deployment conditions can differ from those represented in the records, motivating evaluation against a range of possible distributions. Existing distributionally robust approaches rely on weighting by action probabilities, which can introduce unfavorable variance and estimation behavior.

The paper develops doubly robust algorithms for uncertainty sets defined through KL divergence. Its evaluation algorithm uses localization so that only a small number of regressions must be fitted. Under weak conditions on products of estimation rates, it achieves semiparametric efficiency. This supplies a statistical efficiency result while retaining a manageable regression workload.

For policy learning, a second algorithm achieves regret of order one over the square root of the sample size under a product-rate condition involving a continuum of regressions. The result allows unknown action probabilities to be estimated nonparametrically. Simulations support the methods, and the authors extend their results to general f-divergence uncertainty sets. The guarantees remain tied to their stated estimation-rate conditions.
icml-2022-doubly-robust-distributionally.tldr: Doubly robust methods improve the statistical guarantees of off-policy evaluation and learning under specified distribution-shift uncertainty sets and estimation conditions.

paragraphs: A stationary kernel can be described through its frequency-domain spectral density. Modeling that density with a Gaussian mixture produces a Spectral Mixture kernel, a flexible family capable of modeling any stationary kernel. However, fitting its many parameters can create scalability and overfitting problems, making that expressiveness difficult to use effectively.

The paper proposes an approximate inference procedure for the kernel’s hyperparameters. It replaces the kernel with an approximation built from finitely many random spectral points using Random Fourier Features. Sampling-based variational inference then optimizes the distribution from which those points are drawn. This shifts parameter estimation into a representation based on sampled frequencies.

The authors analyze the training loss and introduce two refinements to the procedure. One changes how spectral points are sampled to reduce kernel approximation error during training. The other uses an approximate natural gradient to accelerate convergence of parameter inference. Together, these components address two distinct obstacles: representing the kernel accurately with finite samples and optimizing the resulting model efficiently.
icml-2022-efficient-approximate-inferenc.tldr: The paper fits Spectral Mixture kernels through sampled frequencies, with refinements targeting approximation error and optimization speed.

paragraphs: Machine learning frameworks have grown alongside the computational demands of the models they support. Their size and complexity can make it difficult to experiment with new ways of performing computation. The paper argues that framework design should serve systems researchers as well as researchers and practitioners who mainly use frameworks to train models.

Flashlight is an open-source library designed around that goal. It provides modular, customizable internals together with research-ready models and training setups across multiple domains. This combination gives researchers places to modify the computational machinery while retaining realistic machine learning workloads on which to try their ideas. The intended benefit is faster prototyping of innovations in tools and systems.

The authors report low overhead and performance that competes with, and often exceeds, popular machine learning frameworks. They position Flashlight as infrastructure for research whose results could later benefit widely used libraries. Its broader contribution is to connect framework experimentation with practical model training, helping systems and machine learning researchers work on shared computational problems.
icml-2022-flashlight-enabling-innovation.tldr: Flashlight pairs customizable framework internals with research-ready models to make machine learning systems experimentation easier and computationally competitive.

paragraphs: An image classifier can rely on familiar surroundings when deciding what an object is. If training data rarely shows objects in unusual settings, a model may predict an object associated with the background instead of recognizing the one present. FOCUS is a dataset designed to test this weakness directly.

The authors deliberately collect images of familiar objects in both common and uncommon contexts using search engines. The collection spans locations, weather conditions, and times of day. Evaluating popular image classifiers on these images reveals a clear accuracy drop in uncommon settings. This makes the dataset a way to examine how recognition changes when contextual expectations become unreliable.

The paper also reports that fine-tuning on FOCUS substantially improves models’ ability to attend to the intended object and generalize better. Beyond evaluation and training, the authors use FOCUS to automatically annotate additional visual attributes throughout ImageNet. Together, these contributions provide data and analysis for investigating contextual dependence and improving robustness to changes in the settings where objects appear.
icml-2022-focus-familiar-objects-in-comm.tldr: FOCUS exposes image classifiers’ difficulty with familiar objects in unusual settings and shows that targeted fine-tuning improves generalization.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire tasks sequentially while preserving what it learned earlier. Winning SubNetworks, or WSN, approaches this by learning and selecting a separate subnetwork for each task within a dense network. The motivation comes from the idea that competitive smaller networks can exist inside a larger one.

WSN jointly learns network weights and task-specific binary masks that determine which weights participate in each subnetwork. It seeks small active weight sets while reusing weights from earlier subnetworks. The stated protection against catastrophic forgetting comes from preventing a selected task subnetwork from interfering with the others. Reuse and preservation are therefore both central to how tasks share the network.

The method also addresses the storage needed to record each task’s selection. It combines the binary masks into an N-bit representation and compresses that representation using Huffman coding. The paper states that this produces sub-linear growth in network capacity with the number of tasks. The contribution couples a noninterfering subnetwork construction with a compact way to retain task-specific routing information.
icml-2022-forget-free-continual-learning.tldr: WSN preserves sequentially learned tasks through noninterfering subnetworks and compresses the masks that select each task’s weights.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to optimize convex objectives privately when data can have heavy tails. Much previous work assumes a Lipschitz loss, which restricts how quickly the loss can change. Here, the authors instead consider general convex losses under an assumption that the gradient distribution has a bounded kth moment.

Under concentrated differential privacy, they improve upper bounds on excess population risk for both convex and strongly convex losses. This quantity measures how far the learned solution’s population objective is from the optimum. As part of the development, they introduce algorithms for privately estimating the mean of heavy-tailed distributions under both pure and concentrated differential privacy.

The paper also proves nearly matching lower bounds for private mean estimation and optimization with strongly convex losses. These bounds show how close the achievable guarantees are to fundamental limits in the analyzed settings. They additionally reveal new separations between pure and concentrated privacy. Thus, the work clarifies both algorithmic possibilities and how the chosen privacy definition affects statistical performance under the stated moment assumption.
icml-2022-improved-rates-for-differentia.tldr: Under bounded gradient moments, the paper improves private convex optimization guarantees and establishes nearly matching limits for key heavy-tailed estimation problems.

paragraphs: Fairness guarantees can depend on training and deployment data following the same distribution. FairSmooth addresses this dependence by constructing a group-fairness certificate that is independent of the input domain. The method is intended to improve classification fairness while maintaining strong prediction accuracy.

Its construction smooths base classifiers using Gaussian parameter smoothing. It learns an individual smoothed classifier for each group using that group’s data, then averages the individual classifiers’ parameters to produce an overall classifier. Group-specific learning and parameter averaging are therefore explicit parts of the proposed procedure, rather than fairness being considered only after training.

The theoretical argument represents the smoothed classifiers through a Nemytskii operator, a mathematical framework for analyzing the resulting output functions. The authors show that this operator is smooth and induces a differentiable manifold. Crucially, they establish a global Lipschitz constant for that manifold that does not depend on the input domain. This domain-independent bound is what yields the paper’s input-agnostic group-fairness certificate and distinguishes its guarantee from distribution-dependent approaches.
icml-2022-input-agnostic-certified-group.tldr: FairSmooth combines Gaussian parameter smoothing and group-specific classifiers to derive a group-fairness certificate independent of the input domain.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning has achieved strong results in many settings, but applying it to complex physical machinery remains difficult. This paper demonstrates its use for optimizing a linear particle accelerator. The setting is only partially observable, meaning the optimization must proceed without a complete view of the machine’s state.

A central feature of the demonstration is that learning does not require training on the real accelerator. The reported method nevertheless operates successfully on the real machine. This brings together two practical challenges: preparing a learning-based optimizer without real-machine training and using it when the available observations provide incomplete information about the system.

In the reported comparison, the method outperforms conventional optimization algorithms in both the achieved result and the time required, while approaching human-level performance. These findings establish the feasibility of the approach for the demonstrated accelerator task. The authors further anticipate that automation could improve machine availability and operability, with benefits for fields using accelerators. Those broader operational benefits are presented as expectations rather than measured outcomes of the study.
icml-2022-learning-based-optimisation-of.tldr: A reinforcement learning method optimizes a real linear particle accelerator under partial observability without training on the real machine.

paragraphs: A learned controller may behave reliably on familiar inputs yet produce errors when its actions carry it into unfamiliar situations. This paper seeks a way to keep both the system’s states and the controller’s actions close to the distribution represented in training. The concern extends across the full sequence of decisions made during deployment.

The proposed Lyapunov density models combine ideas from control theory and density estimation. Lyapunov stability and control-invariant sets provide tools for reasoning about whether a controller can keep a system within desired regions. Density models describe where training data is concentrated. Combining these perspectives connects familiarity with the data to the system’s ability to remain in familiar conditions.

The resulting construction generalizes control Lyapunov functions and density models. Its stated contribution is a guarantee about an agent’s ability to stay within the training distribution throughout its trajectory, using actions that are also in-distribution. This matters because familiarity at one moment does not by itself resolve what subsequent decisions will do; the proposed framework explicitly addresses that continuing control problem.
icml-2022-lyapunov-density-models-constr.tldr: Lyapunov density models combine control stability and density estimation to provide guarantees about remaining in-distribution throughout a controlled trajectory.

paragraphs: A neural network can be viewed as a structural causal model describing how changes to its inputs affect its output. However, training for prediction accuracy on data containing both causal and correlational relationships does not ensure that these learned effects match real causal relationships. The paper uses expert knowledge to guide those effects during training.

The proposed regularizer aligns a network’s learned causal effects with supplied domain priors. It accommodates both direct and total effects, as well as different forms of prior knowledge. Examples include requiring an effect to be monotonic or requiring a variable to have zero causal effect on the output for a fairness objective. This makes desired input-output behavior an explicit training consideration.

Experiments on twelve benchmark datasets show that the method can maintain the desired causal effects without sacrificing accuracy in those evaluations. The authors also report robustness and improved accuracy when inputs are noisy. The findings support regularization as a practical way to incorporate causal expertise into neural networks, with the desired behavior determined by the supplied priors.
icml-2022-matching-learned-causal-effect.tldr: A causal-effect regularizer incorporates domain priors into neural networks while preserving accuracy and improving performance on noisy inputs in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making needs confidence sets that describe uncertainty about prediction functions. These sets often depend on a predefined hypothesis space, such as one determined by a kernel. Choosing that kernel incorrectly can undermine performance or safety. Meta-KeL uses offline data to learn the kernel instead of relying entirely on manual design.

The analysis considers an unknown kernel that is a combination of known base kernels. For this setting, the authors construct an estimator using structured sparsity. Under mild conditions, the estimated reproducing kernel Hilbert space provides valid confidence sets. As more offline data becomes available, those sets become as tight as the ones obtainable with knowledge of the true kernel.

The paper applies the approach to kernelized bandits, also known as Bayesian optimization. It establishes regret bounds competitive with those available under the true kernel and includes an empirical Bayesian optimization evaluation. The contribution connects learning a hypothesis space from previous data with reliable uncertainty estimates for later decisions, under the stated kernel-combination setting and theoretical conditions.
icml-2022-meta-learning-hypothesis-space.tldr: Meta-KeL learns a kernel from offline data and, under stated conditions, obtains valid confidence sets that approach those based on the true kernel.

paragraphs: Quantifying causal contributions means assigning strengths to the different causes of a target outcome. This paper approaches that assignment by first asking what properties a reasonable contribution measure should satisfy. Starting with explicit axioms makes the meaning of the resulting allocation part of the mathematical specification.

The authors introduce do-Shapley values, a contribution measure inspired by causal interventions. They show that it is the unique measure satisfying their proposed properties. This uniqueness is relative to the selected axioms: the result connects those requirements to a particular way of attributing causal influence, giving the measure a principled foundation.

The paper then develops a criterion under which these values can be inferred efficiently from non-experimental data. It also provides estimators with consistency, computational feasibility, and statistical robustness, with simulations supporting the theoretical results. Together, these steps connect the definition of a causal contribution to conditions for recovering it from observations and to practical estimation procedures. The observational inference claim depends on the stated criterion being met.
icml-2022-on-measuring-causal-contributi.tldr: Do-Shapley values uniquely satisfy the paper’s causal-contribution axioms and admit robust estimation from observational data under a specified criterion.

paragraphs: A decoder that predicts behavior from neural recordings can lose accuracy across recording sessions. Individual neurons may change their activity, and probe movement can change which neurons are observed. The paper builds on evidence that the lower-dimensional dynamics underlying behavior may remain stable even while those measured signals change.

The proposed model combines unsupervised domain adaptation with a sequential variational autoencoder trained across several sessions. Its goal is to recover behaviorally relevant latent dynamics from previously unseen recordings of the same animal. This shared latent description supports behavior prediction without requiring the decoder to be recalibrated for each new recording session.

The authors report good generalization to unseen data and successful behavior predictions in cases where conventional methods fail. These results support the hypothesis that behavior-related population dynamics are low-dimensional and stable over time. The same-animal setting is an important part of the claim. The work points toward more flexible brain-computer interfaces by addressing changes in recording conditions while preserving access to the underlying behavioral information.
icml-2022-robust-alignment-of-cross-sess.tldr: Combining unsupervised domain adaptation with a sequential latent-variable model enables behavior prediction across unseen recording sessions from the same animal.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained neural network to a new task, but it can overfit the target data. Keeping the adapted parameters close to their initial values is one known way to improve generalization. This paper investigates how the curvature of the loss, represented by Hessians, adds to that explanation.

Using PAC-Bayesian analysis, the authors connect generalization to both parameter movement and stability under injected noise. They derive Hessian distance-based bounds for a broad range of fine-tuning methods. They then design an algorithm combining consistent losses with distance-based regularization to address noisy labels, and prove a generalization bound under a class-conditional independent label-noise assumption.

The empirical study spans multiple architectures and noisy environments. On six image classification tasks with programmatically generated training labels, the authors report a 3.26% accuracy improvement over prior methods. They also report a six-times-greater decrease in the Hessian distance measure than existing approaches. These findings connect the proposed theoretical measure with improved fine-tuning behavior in the evaluated noisy-label settings.
icml-2022-robust-fine-tuning-of-deep-neu.tldr: Hessian-based analysis motivates a regularized fine-tuning method with conditional noisy-label guarantees and improved accuracy in reported experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops bounds connecting a learning algorithm’s robustness with its ability to generalize beyond training examples. The central change is to make that connection depend more effectively on the observed data. The authors use a property of the training samples that can be observed and computed.

The bounds improve earlier results in two ways: they reduce dependence on the covering number and remove dependence on the hypothesis space. The paper provides examples, including lasso and deep learning, where the new bounds are provably preferable. These are improvements in the theoretical assessment of generalization, with the data-dependent formulation supplying the additional information used in that assessment.

Experiments on real-world data and theoretical models show near-exponential improvements in various situations. The authors obtain these gains without adding assumptions about the unknown data distribution. A key ingredient is a sharper concentration bound for multinomial random variables, which may also be useful beyond this application. The results strengthen the mathematical link between robustness and generalization while keeping the improvements tied to the analyzed settings.
icml-2022-robustness-implies-generalizat.tldr: New data-dependent bounds strengthen the connection between robustness and generalization without additional assumptions on the unknown distribution.

paragraphs: Generating graphs requires capturing how nodes and edges depend on one another while respecting that relabeling nodes does not change the underlying graph. These demands are especially important for molecular graphs, where the relationships between atoms and bonds determine whether a generated structure is plausible.

The paper proposes a continuous-time graph diffusion process that represents nodes and edges jointly through a system of stochastic differential equations. Tailored score-matching objectives learn gradients of the joint log-density with respect to each component. A new solver then samples from the reverse diffusion process efficiently. Modeling the components jointly makes their relationships part of the generation procedure.

Across diverse datasets, the method achieves either significantly better or competitive performance relative to the evaluated baselines. Additional analysis finds that it can generate molecules close to the training distribution without violating chemical valency rules. That result supports the effectiveness of the coupled equations in representing node-edge relationships. It is an empirical finding about the generated molecules, rather than a stated universal chemical-validity guarantee.
icml-2022-score-based-generative-modelin.tldr: A coupled diffusion model learns node-edge relationships jointly and produces competitive graph generation results, including molecules that respect valency in the reported analysis.

paragraphs: Graph learning infers connections between nodes from measurements taken at those nodes. Many methods assume that all observations share one underlying graph. This paper addresses heterogeneous data, where different groups of observations may instead correspond to different graph structures, requiring both the groups and their graphs to be discovered.

The authors formulate clustering and graph inference as a joint optimization problem. Their method extends spectral clustering by considering not only pairwise similarities between graph signals but also how smoothly those signals vary over a candidate cluster graph. It learns a representative graph for each cluster using the same relationship between signal smoothness and graph topology.

This coupling allows the inferred graph structure to inform the grouping of observations, while each group’s signals inform its graph. The resulting problem is solved using an efficient block-coordinate descent algorithm. Results on simulated and real data indicate that the method is effective. The contribution is a unified treatment of two interdependent tasks that arise when a single graph cannot adequately represent all the observations.
icml-2022-simultaneous-graph-signal-clus.tldr: The method jointly clusters heterogeneous graph signals and learns a representative graph for each cluster using similarity and signal smoothness.

paragraphs: Ridge regression balances fitting observations against a penalty on the size of the solution. This paper studies the case where the number of variables is at least the number of observations. It gives an iterative sketching algorithm that achieves an objective value within a factor of one plus epsilon of the optimum.

For a constant number of iterations and input passes, the algorithm weakens the accuracy requirements imposed on the sketching matrix. It needs an epsilon-dependent approximate matrix multiplication guarantee together with a constant subspace embedding guarantee. Earlier work required the subspace embedding guarantee itself to depend on epsilon. This distinction allows a sparser OSNAP embedding at the same stated row count in the one-iteration comparison.

The authors also use the approach to obtain faster algorithms for kernel ridge regression. Lower bounds show that its required sketch size is essentially optimal within a natural framework of ridge regression algorithms. Those bounds concern oblivious sketches for approximate matrix multiplication, so their significance extends to understanding the compression requirements of that underlying computational task.
icml-2022-sketching-algorithms-and-lower.tldr: A ridge regression sketching algorithm weakens sketch requirements while retaining approximation guarantees, with essentially optimal sketch size within the analyzed framework.

paragraphs: This paper explores a network architecture for meta-learning in which units compete locally to produce an activation. The units are arranged into blocks, and only one unit in each block contributes a nonzero output. As a result, each layer produces a sparse representation rather than activating all of its competing units.

The winning unit is chosen stochastically through posterior sampling. Randomness is therefore part of how the network builds its representations, alongside the sparsity imposed by local competition. The proposed design makes this sparse, stochastic representation mechanism a central component of the model used for learning across tasks.

The authors report state-of-the-art predictive accuracy in their few-shot image classification and regression experiments, as well as lower prediction error in an active learning setting. They also report a very large reduction in computational cost. These findings indicate that, in the evaluated tasks, stochastic local competition can support strong predictions while reducing computation. The contribution combines an architectural change with empirical evidence across several forms of learning from limited information.
icml-2022-stochastic-deep-networks-with-.tldr: Networks with stochastic local winner-takes-all units achieve strong reported meta-learning results while substantially reducing computational cost.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection identifies inputs that differ from the data a classifier is intended to handle. Some training approaches use auxiliary outlier data while assuming it is completely separable from in-distribution data. This paper instead uses the mixed stream of familiar and unfamiliar examples that naturally appears during deployment.

The authors formulate learning as a constrained optimization problem. The objective maximizes detection of out-of-distribution examples, while constraints control classification error on in-distribution data and the rate at which those familiar examples are incorrectly flagged as outliers. This formulation explicitly balances detecting unfamiliar inputs with preserving useful behavior on the classifier’s intended inputs.

The paper shows how to solve the optimization problem tractably and evaluates the approach extensively on common out-of-distribution detection tasks. It reports superior performance in those evaluations. The practical significance is that training can use naturally occurring mixture data instead of requiring an auxiliary collection assumed to consist of cleanly separated outliers. The constraints make the competing goals of classification and detection part of the learning objective.
icml-2022-training-ood-detectors-in-thei.tldr: A constrained training framework learns OOD detection from naturally mixed deployment data while controlling errors on in-distribution examples.
